character_and_relationship_context: Ingrid Solberg is a fish processing business owner. She inherited money from her grandmother, a formidable woman who ran a salting shed in the 1960s. That inheritance bought her loft, industrial chillers, and modern smokehouses. She grew up on the docks, the only girl among boys, after her mother left when she was twelve, learning the fish business from her father's hands and ruthlessness from her grandmother. Her father is seventy-four with vascular dementia, living in a nearby flat with rotating caregivers whom Ingrid manages. She audits caregiver logs, verifying details like the exact time of her father's last insulin dose. She sold her father's boat to pay for the loft; he remembers the boat and hates that she sold it. She keeps an engine bolt from that boat on her windowsill, touching it every morning before turning on the smokers. She reads Norwegian poetry aloud to her father on afternoon visits even when he does not recognize her. She is fiercely vocal about margins and quality but utterly private about her family's erosion. She manages the caregivers, competition prep, and nine-person payroll, monitoring through logbooks, spreadsheets, and the smell of smoked fish. She tests brine percentages at 4 AM, re-smokes a batch if color is off, and confronts suppliers harshly. Competitor pricing spreadsheets go only to two of her nine employees, Håkon and Mette; the other seven smoke and salt fish but are kept ignorant of her strategy. She reminds workers of dugnad—the collective village effort—but quietly subverts it. She speaks in her hometown dialect even to major food critics. She tends to decline weekend invitations that overlap with production prep, having skipped three dock gatherings this season. Sundays follow a fixed order: smokehouse walk, father visit, then anything else. She contributes to dugnad with supplies rather than time. Lars is a retired neighbor who once crewed with her father; he sends weather jokes weekly and has not pushed when she misses his dock gatherings. Her father's illness defines their fragile daily rhythm; she audits his caregivers and visits every afternoon, carrying quiet guilt about selling his boat.
objective_situation: On a bright Sunday morning, Ingrid is at the loft reviewing brine charts when her retired neighbor, Lars, knocks on the door. He tells her that a few people from the dock are taking his old boat out to fish along the fjord, a traditional excursion she remembers from her childhood. He offers her a spare rod and a spot onboard. Ingrid knows that joining would mean losing a few hours of weekend work on her competition prep, but it also offers a rare chance to reconnect with the pastime her father loved and the local customs she grew up with.
state_and_available_memories: She has been up since 4 AM testing brine and reviewing Week 14 pricing; eyes tired, hands steady. Sunday's smokehouse walk is still pending, and the afternoon father visit is scheduled, leaving only the morning open. No urgent quality or payroll issue is pending; the loft is quiet, smelling of fresh smoke. Immediate memories: Lars's old boat evokes summer Sundays on her father's fjord cruiser, coiling rope and listening to men argue over herring runs. The tarred rope smell in the loft is her childhood cue, but today it brings her father's hands on the tiller before the dementia. Reflective memories: She has not been on the fjord since selling her father's boat for the loft; only the engine bolt on the windowsill remains. Her grandmother called the fjord 'the first ledger,' a phrase Ingrid still repeats when she reads tides. Her father said a Sunday on the water was fuel, not lost work, though she has long counted hours differently.
name: Ingrid Solberg
